title: Why Current Approaches Fail
use_cases: Use when diagnosing why early readers are abandoning a manuscript before chapter three
Configure when establishing character routines to ensure they provide narrative value rather than boredom
Implement when transitioning from an intuitive writing style to a structured, craft-based approach
Use when evaluating whether an opening sequence creates sufficient investment before introducing backstory
Configure when balancing prose aesthetics with structural narrative requirements
content:
Hook them with a great first line = gimmicky, and insufficient on the how.

Start with action = sometimes confusing, often fails to create investment, works better in movies.

The story finds it’s feet by chapter 3 = readers are already gone.

The opening of a story is too-often treated like a set-up for the actual story.

We want to avoid front-loading backstory and beginning with too much exposition, sure. That’s common advice, and the reason is simple: you’re adding more cognitive load than readers can handle before they have a reason to care.

Unless your prose is beautiful and the reader enjoys beautiful prose more than story, exposition and backstory are just asking them to learn facts about your story in order to enjoy it, and that’s backwards.

Starting with the character’s “ordinary life” is something I see recommended a lot, and it’s necessary so they can “return changed” at the end if you follow that story structure, but…

Ordinary doesn’t mean boring.

I read a lot of pieces where the character wakes up and begins their day—a boring, routine day that is the same as many of us have: brush teeth, make coffee, check phone.

No.

You want to establish their ordinary life, but you also want to establish the tone, style, and promise your story is making to the reader. The regular routine tells us nothing about what type of story this will be.

You can be both setting up the overall story and telling a story, at the same time.

How?

I prefer to think of the opening as having a measurable structure with specific milestones.

But don’t tune out if you’re a discovery writer! I’m not saying you have to plot anything in advance. Plotters can use this to guide their work ahead of time, and pantsers can use it as a diagnostic tool for a wandering openings after they finish writing.

So what is the structure and what are the milestones we want to hit?

The opening is not where you ease into the story.

It’s where you win the reader’s attention and trust, and earn their commitment.

You can build your opening with intention instead of hope, transforming it from mysterious intuition into solid craft.

You’ll know exactly where the opening isn’t working and reduce reader abandonment by delivering on promises at each structural milestone.

There are three thresholds we’ll be looking at: the micro, meso, and macro.
